refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.para: udevd listens to kernel uevents. For every event, udevd executes matching instructions specified in udev rules. See udev7 .
The behavior of the daemon can be configured using udev.conf5, its command-line options, environment variables, and on the kernel command-line, or changed dynamically with udevadm control.

On SIGTERM or SIGINT, or with udevadm control --exit, udevd discards the queued events, tells its workers to exit, and waits up to 30 seconds for the events being processed. A worker that has not finished its event 5 seconds later is killed with SIGKILL.

listitem.para: Detach and run in the background. Unless the log level is debug, standard input, output and error are connected to /dev/null; then, unlike systemd, which writes them to /dev/null, the messages for the console, e.g. with the console log target of $SYSTEMD_LOG_TARGET or systemd.log_target= on the kernel command line, are written to /dev/console, or, when that cannot be opened, e.g. in a container, to the kernel log buffer (/dev/kmsg).
Print debug messages to standard error. The log level set with udev.log_level= on the kernel command line takes precedence over it.

Issue (S6/dinit compatible) readiness notification via a file descriptor. A short message followed by a newline character will be sent via the specified file descriptor (inherited from the parent process) when initialization is complete.

Limit the number of events executed in parallel. When it is not specified or 0, the maximum is determined based on the system resources: MIN(2 × CPUs + 16, MAX(RAM / 128 MiB, 10), 2048), where CPUs is the number of CPUs udevd may run on, according to its CPU affinity, and RAM the size of the physical memory, or the memory limit of the cgroup of PID 1 when it is smaller: memory.max with cgroup v2, or memory.limit_in_bytes in the hierarchy of the memory controller with cgroup v1. It takes precedence over children_max= in udev.conf5, unless it is 0.

Delay the execution of RUN instructions by the given number of seconds, or by a time span with a unit, e.g. 500ms. This option might be useful when debugging system crashes during coldplug caused by loading non-working kernel modules. A delay that is not shorter than the event timeout is ignored. It takes precedence over exec_delay= in udev.conf5, unless it is 0.

Set the number of seconds to wait for events to finish, or a time span with a unit, e.g. 5min. After this time the event will be terminated. The default is 180 seconds, which is also used when 0 or less than a millisecond is given. It takes precedence over event_timeout= in udev.conf5, unless it is 0.

When the timeout is reached, the worker processing the event sends the timeout signal (see --timeout-signal=) to the program of RUN, PROGRAM or IMPORT{program} that is still running. If the worker has not finished the event 10 seconds later, udevd sends the timeout signal to the worker. This extra time can be set with the $UDEV_EXTRA_TIMEOUT_SEC environment variable of udevd, or $SYSTEMD_UDEV_EXTRA_TIMEOUT_SEC when that is not set, to a time span of up to 5 hours, e.g. 30s.

Set the signal which udevd will send to forked off processes after reaching event timeout. The setting can be overridden at boot time with the kernel command line option udev.timeout_signal=. Setting to SIGABRT may be helpful in order to debug worker timeouts. Defaults to SIGKILL. Note that setting the option on the command line overrides the setting from the configuration file. The signal is given as a number or a name, with or without the SIG prefix. Signals whose default action does not terminate a process, with which the timeout would not stop anything, are ignored with a warning: SIGCHLD, SIGCONT, SIGSTOP, SIGTSTP, SIGTTIN, SIGTTOU, SIGURG and SIGWINCH. A worker that has not finished its event 5 seconds after the signal, e.g. as it blocks SIGTERM while it processes an event, is killed with SIGKILL; after a signal whose default action dumps core, e.g. SIGABRT, 90 seconds, so that the core dump is not cut off.

Specify when udevd should resolve names of users and groups. When set to early (the default), names will be resolved when the rules are parsed. When set to late, names will be resolved for every event. When set to never, names will never be resolved, and the OWNER and GROUP keys whose value is not a numeric ID, i.e. a name or a value with substitutions, will be ignored; the other keys of these rules still apply. It takes precedence over resolve_names= in udev.conf5.
Print a short help text and exit.
Print a short version string and exit.

refsect1.title: Kernel command line

variablelist.para: Parameters starting with "rd." will be read when udevd is used in an initrd, and are ignored otherwise, also by IMPORT{cmdline} in the rules. As in systemd, udevd considers itself running in an initrd when /etc/initrd-release exists. As initrds that are not made for systemd do not provide /etc/initrd-release, unlike systemd it also does so when the root file system is a memory file system (the rootfs of an initramfs, i.e. ramfs or tmpfs), /init exists, and one of the files that such initrd generators put into the initrd exists: /conf/initramfs.conf (initramfs-tools), /lib/dracut-lib.sh (dracut before version 019), /init_functions (old versions of mkinitcpio), /etc/initrd.defaults (genkernel before version 4.2) or /.modloop (mkinitfs of Alpine Linux). The detection can be overridden with the $SYSTEMD_IN_INITRD environment variable, set to a boolean value.

In the names of the parameters, "-" and "_" are the same, e.g. udev.children-max= is the same as udev.children_max=. Like systemd, udevd warns about other parameters that start with udev., e.g. misspelled ones, and, in an initrd, with rd.udev., and ignores them.

listitem.para: Set the log level. udev.log_priority= and rd.udev.log_priority= are accepted too. It takes precedence over udev_log= in udev.conf5 and over --debug, and udevadm control --log-level= takes precedence over it.
Enable/disable trace logging. When enabled, udev.log_level= will be ignored, and debug level is assumed.
Limit the number of events executed in parallel. It takes precedence over --children-max=, unless it is 0. See --children-max= for the default.

Delay the execution of RUN instructions by the given number of seconds, or by a time span with a unit, e.g. 500ms. This option might be useful when debugging system crashes during coldplug caused by loading non-working kernel modules. It takes precedence over --exec-delay=, unless it is 0.

Wait for events to finish up to the given number of seconds, or a time span with a unit, e.g. 5min. This option might be useful if events are terminated due to kernel drivers taking too long to initialize. It takes precedence over --event-timeout=, unless it is 0.

Specifies a signal that udevd will send to workers on timeout. Note that kernel command line option overrides both the setting in the configuration file and the one on the program command line. As with --timeout-signal=, signals that do not terminate a process are ignored with a warning.

If specified, mark all physical block devices read-only as they appear. Synthetic block devices (such as loopback block devices or device mapper devices) are left as they are. This is useful to guarantee that the contents of physical block devices remains unmodified during runtime, for example to implement fully stateless systems, for testing or for recovery situations where corrupted file systems shall not be corrupted further through accidental modification.
A block device may be marked writable again by issuing the blockdev --setrw command, see blockdev8 for details.

Network interfaces are renamed to give them predictable names when possible. It is enabled by default; specifying 0 disables it. When eudev is built with --with-net-ifnames-default=no, it is disabled by default; specifying 1 enables it, and also the alternative names of network interfaces, which are then only assigned with 1. When eudev is built with --enable-rule-generator, the rule generator keeps the names that the kernel gave the interfaces: by default, 80-net-name-slot.rules, which renames the interfaces, is not installed, as the rule generator replaces it, and this option changes nothing; when eudev is also built with --with-net-ifnames-default=no, specifying 1 enables the renaming, as without the rule generator, except for the interfaces that its rules name already, and the rule generator then records no names (see udev7).

Selects the naming scheme, i.e. the version of the naming logic of the net_id builtin, that is used to generate the predictable names of network interfaces. It takes the name of a scheme: eudev for the names generated by net_id of eudev 3.2.15 and older, one of the schemes of systemd v238, v239, v240, v241, v243, v245, v247, v249, v250, v251, v252, v253, v254, v255, v257, v258, v259, v260 and v261, or latest for the latest one, which is the default. The schemes are described in udev7. This option takes precedence over net_naming_scheme= in udev.conf5. The $NET_NAMING_SCHEME environment variable of udevd takes precedence over both, unless its value starts with :.

Like in systemd, the same as the environment variables $SYSTEMD_LOG_LEVEL, $SYSTEMD_LOG_TARGET, $SYSTEMD_LOG_COLOR, $SYSTEMD_LOG_LOCATION, $SYSTEMD_LOG_TIME, $SYSTEMD_LOG_TID and $SYSTEMD_LOG_RATELIMIT_KMSG, see below, which take precedence over them. Like in systemd, debug without a value is the same as systemd.log_level=debug. Like systemd before version 248, every program of eudev that has no controlling terminal reads them: udevd, the programs that it runs, e.g. udevadm or helpers like scsi_id, and the commands run without a terminal, e.g. by init scripts; a command run from a terminal ignores them.

refsect1.para: For testing, the kernel command line can be replaced by the value of the $UDEV_PROC_CMDLINE environment variable of udevd and udevadm, when it is set, even to an empty string. It applies to the options described here, to the net.ifnames= option used by 80-net-name-slot.rules (and by 80-net-altnames.rules when eudev is built with --with-net-ifnames-default=no, and by 75-persistent-net-generator.rules when it is also built with --enable-rule-generator), and to IMPORT{cmdline} in the rules in general, and it is handled like the kernel command line, e.g. options starting with "rd." are ignored outside of an initrd:
refsect1.programlisting: UDEV_PROC_CMDLINE="net.naming_scheme=v250" udevadm test-builtin net_id /sys/class/net/eth0 UDEV_PROC_CMDLINE="net.ifnames=0" udevadm test /sys/class/net/eth0 UDEV_PROC_CMDLINE="net.ifnames=1" udevadm test /sys/class/net/eth0
refsect1.para: The last two commands show what the rules do with the interface when the renaming is disabled and when it is enabled, independent of the default of net.ifnames= that eudev is built with. They do not run write_net_rules, the program of the rule generator, so they do not show a name that it would give.
For compatibility with systemd, $SYSTEMD_PROC_CMDLINE is used the same way when $UDEV_PROC_CMDLINE is not set.

refsect1.title: Environment
refsect1.para: Each of the following settings is read from $UDEV_LOG_NAME, e.g. $UDEV_LOG_LEVEL, and, like in systemd, from $SYSTEMD_LOG_NAME, e.g. $SYSTEMD_LOG_LEVEL, when the former is not set. udevadm reads them too, see udevadm8.

listitem.para: The maximum log level of emitted messages (messages with a higher log level, i.e. less important ones, are suppressed). Takes a comma-separated list of values. A value may be either one of (in order of decreasing importance) emerg, alert, crit, err, warning, notice, info, debug, or an integer in the range 0…7, also with a 0x, 0o or 0b prefix. See syslog3 for more information. Each value may optionally be prefixed with one of console, syslog or kmsg followed by a colon to set the maximum log level for that specific log target (e.g. SYSTEMD_LOG_LEVEL=debug,console:info specifies to log at debug level except when logging to the console which should be at info level). Note that the global maximum log level takes priority over any per target maximum log levels. Like in systemd, it takes precedence over systemd.log_level= on the kernel command line, and udev_log= of udev.conf5, --debug, udev.log_level= on the kernel command line and udevadm control --log-level= take precedence over it.

The destination for log messages. One of console (log to the attached tty), console-prefixed (log to the attached tty but with prefixes encoding the log level and "facility", see syslog3), kmsg (log to the kernel circular log buffer), syslog (log to /dev/log), syslog-or-kmsg (log to /dev/log if available, and to kmsg otherwise), auto (log to kmsg if it can be written, and to the attached tty otherwise), safe (log to kmsg if standard error is not a tty, and to the attached tty otherwise), null (disable log output). The default is auto; --debug logs to the console.

A boolean. If true, messages written to the tty are colored according to their log level, like in systemd: errors and more important ones in red, warnings in yellow, notices highlighted and debug messages in grey. The default is true. Colors are used only when standard output and standard error are terminals, and $TERM is set and not dumb, and $NO_COLOR and $SYSTEMD_COLORS are used like by udevadm, see udevadm8.

A boolean. If true, messages written to the tty are prefixed with a filename and line number in the source code where the message originates. The filename is relative to the top of the source tree, e.g. src/udev/udevd.c, like in systemd.
A boolean. If true, messages written to the tty are prefixed with the local time, e.g. Mon 2026-10-05 12:34:56 EEST, like in systemd.
A boolean. If true, messages written to the tty are prefixed with the numerical thread ID (TID) in parentheses, like in systemd.

A boolean, true by default. If true, like in systemd, at most 200 messages in 5 seconds are written to the kernel log buffer by each process; the first message that is dropped is replaced by Too many messages being logged to kmsg, ignoring. If false, the messages written to kmsg are not rate limited.
